html:
The Indian Removal Act was a United States law signed by President Andrew Jackson on 28 May 1830. It let the president trade land west of the Mississippi for the lands of Native nations in the east, and paid for moving them.

The law spoke of voluntary exchange. In practice treaties were forced, signed by small factions, or ignored, and the army moved people at gunpoint. The main targets were the large nations of the Southeast, whose land cotton planters wanted: the Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Cherokee and Seminole.

  • The Choctaw went first, from 1831, after the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek.
  • The Muscogee were forced out in 1836 and 1837.
  • The Cherokee won in the Supreme Court in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), but the ruling was not enforced. In 1838 and 1839 soldiers drove them west on the Trail of Tears, and thousands died.
  • The Seminole fought back in the Second Seminole War of 1835 to 1842.
  • In the north the Potawatomi, Shawnee and others were moved too.

The removed nations were settled in "Indian Territory", in today's Oklahoma. Tens of thousands of people lost their homes, and millions of acres in the Southeast were opened to white settlers and to cotton grown by enslaved people.
